title: Pyongyang Fires Hypersonic IRBM as Lockheed Weighs Building Patriot Interceptors Abroad
subhead: North Korea tested a medium-range hypersonic missile and Kim Jong Un framed it as 'nuclear deterrence in action', while Lockheed Martin confirmed advanced talks to move Patriot PAC-3 production outside the US to meet tripled global demand.

sections.heading: North Korea Tests Hypersonic IRBM, Kim Frames It as Deterrence
sections.body:
North Korea conducted a medium-range strategic missile launch drill from its eastern region toward the East Sea on October 3, according to the state-run Korean Central News Agency, with leader Kim Jong Un observing on site. KCNA said the drill was 'part of efforts to train the fire-duty capabilities of missile troops handling hypersonic strategic weapons systems, and to evaluate the reliability, effectiveness, and operability of war deterrence' (Chosun Biz translation of Rodong Sinmun).

KCNA claimed the missile hit its designated target point roughly 1,000 km out over the East Sea and released a photo of the round bearing the number 17701922. Kim said improving weapons performance is 'a form of exercising nuclear deterrence', and called for uninterrupted efforts 'to make our adversaries constantly and repeatedly recognize the reliability and lethality of strategic offensive means' (KCNA, via Chosun Biz).

This follows September 20 reporting, tracked by Janes and Defence Express (Defence-UA), of an earlier test of the Hwasong-11Ma-1, a solid-fuel missile with a hypersonic glide vehicle with estimated body length 9.6 m, launch mass 9.8 tons and a recorded range of 908 km flown mostly in glider phase. Janes assessed the September event as a single missile type, not two, correcting early reports.
sections.whyItMatters: North Korea is now routinely demonstrating a mobile, hypersonic-glider missile designed to complicate Patriot and THAAD interception, and Kim is explicitly tying each test to nuclear-deterrence messaging rather than to a negotiating track. That raises the interceptor-demand problem for US and allied air defense at exactly the moment Washington is telling partners to expect multi-year arms delays.

sections.heading: Lockheed in Advanced Talks to Build Patriot PAC-3 Outside the US
sections.body:
Lockheed Martin is in advanced negotiations with several allied countries to establish Patriot PAC-3 production sites abroad, according to Army Recognition, citing a September 30 Kyiv Post interview with Dan Tenney, Lockheed's senior vice president for Global Business Development and Strategy. Tenney described the discussions as 'pretty deep' but said no agreement has been announced and declined to name the countries involved.

The driver is demand: Army Recognition reports that worldwide demand for PAC-3 has tripled, and the US is aiming to lift annual PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement output from roughly 600 to 2,000 interceptors by the end of 2030. This builds on the Pentagon's August 31 framework agreements with General Dynamics and Lockheed to triple PAC-3 MSE and quadruple THAAD interceptor capacity under seven-year deals, with funding still subject to annual congressional appropriations (AeroTime).

The production squeeze is being felt operationally. The Associated Press reported this week that Patriot interceptor shortages continue to constrain Ukrainian air defenses, partly because Middle East operations are competing for the same high-end rounds.
sections.whyItMatters: Moving interceptor assembly to allied soil is the clearest sign yet that the US has accepted it cannot meet global air-defense demand from domestic lines alone. It reshapes the industrial map of missile defense — turning buyers like Japan or European states into co-producers — while doing nothing to close the near-term gap that Ukraine and Gulf partners face now.

sections.heading: Raytheon's $24.4B SM-6 Deal Caps a Record Year of Munitions Orders
sections.body:
The Pentagon awarded Raytheon a $24.4 billion contract to accelerate SM-6 production, a five-year agreement with two option years, TRT World reported. The Navy framed it as securing a 'steady and reliable supply' of the SM-6, a dual-role weapon used for both offensive strikes and missile defense, built in Huntsville, Alabama.

The award follows a $20.7 billion multi-year AMRAAM deal in late September and a $58.6 billion Patriot interceptor package to Lockheed Martin in July (TRT World). The Pentagon's inspector general found that munitions expended during the four-month campaign against Iran, Operation Epic Fury, caused 'strategic inventory shortfalls' and exposed 'industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply'. A September 15 Congressional Budget Office report warned the drawdown 'will leave the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years'.

Separately, Army Recognition and other outlets reported that ball screw shortages are among the specific component bottlenecks constraining PAC-3 and Tomahawk output — a reminder that much of the capacity problem sits with sub-tier suppliers, not prime contractors.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now converting combat expenditure into the largest sustained munitions-buying streak in decades, but the deals are multi-year by design — meaning the inventory hole stays open through the mid-2020s and shapes how much Washington can support Ukraine, the Gulf and Taiwan simultaneously.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Prepares Yemen Offensive to Reopen Bab el-Mandeb
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia is preparing an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi forces to retake the Bab el-Mandeb strait, with Riyadh weighing either a focused coastal assault or a broader operation across Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf, Reuters reported. Six people familiar with the plans, including Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats, said timing ranges from within a week to after the US midterm elections in early November. More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilised, with the operation led by Yemeni forces under Saudi oversight and backed by Saudi air strikes.

The Houthis advanced down the coast last month and seized the strait. Bab el-Mandeb has gained importance as an alternative shipping route amid the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran conflict. Michael Ratney, a former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told Reuters he expects a limited operation to retake coastal areas rather than the scale of the 2015 Saudi-led intervention.

The offensive would be the first real test of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August. Turkey said on September 19 it was prepared to meet Saudi military needs under the pact; Pakistan appointed the arrangement's first secretary-general days later; and the three countries' military chiefs met in Riyadh on September 25 to discuss intelligence sharing and capability integration (Al-Monitor, Saudi Gazette, Dawn).
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is shifting from relying on US security guarantees toward an institutionalized Gulf-Asian defense bloc, and the Bab el-Mandeb operation is where that pact's promise will be tested in practice. A prolonged campaign also reopens demand for air-defense, drones and maritime systems that Turkey and Pakistan are positioned to fill.

sections.heading: India Confirms Akash Exports to Three Central Asian and Caucasus Buyers
sections.body:
Indian Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the export of the indigenous Akash air defense system to Armenia, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, calling it 'one of our success stories' and evidence of a maturing indigenous missile design and production base. Armenia was the first customer and took multiple batteries, with production now described as stabilized, The News Mill reported.

The Akash is a short-range surface-to-air missile built by DRDO with Bharat Dynamics Limited and Bharat Electronics Limited, engaging supersonic targets at 25-30 km; the Akash-NG variant extends to about 50 km with ramjet propulsion and command guidance. Singh said the Ministry of Defence expects exports to reach Rs 50,000 crore within two years, with the BrahMos cruise missile as India's flagship export product (The News Mill; Financial Express reported India's missile exports have crossed a $600 million surge).
sections.whyItMatters: India is converting the Akash from a domestic workhorse into a price-competitive export line aimed at buyers the US and Europe cannot supply quickly. Sales into the Caucasus and Central Asia also give New Delhi a defense-industrial foothold in regions where Russia has historically been the sole supplier.

sections.heading: Russia's 2027 Defense Budget Hits $202B as EU Rearmament Lags Its Own Rhetoric
sections.body:
Russia plans to raise defense spending to 17.1 trillion roubles ($202.6 billion) in 2027, roughly a 27 percent increase over the 13.5 trillion roubles originally allocated, according to budget documents reviewed by Reuters and reported by Military Watch Magazine. The three-year 2027-2029 defense total is projected at about 50 trillion roubles — the highest level of Russian defense spending in over 30 years — with Moscow preparing higher borrowing and taxes to fund it.

On the European side, a CSG analysis highlighted by Around Prague argues Europe's rearmament 'doesn't match the threat of war', and a late-September study reported by Stars and Stripes warned of a years-long European defense gap as the US scales back forces on the continent. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius defended Germany's record 2027 military budget in September (Anadolu Agency).
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is funding a structurally larger military while European spending, despite headline increases, is still described by analysts as lagging the threat and dependent on a US presence that is shrinking. The gap between announced budgets and delivered capability remains the central risk in European defense planning.

bottomLine: North Korea's hypersonic IRBM test and Lockheed's push to build Patriot interceptors abroad point at the same problem from opposite ends: demand for advanced air-defense and strike missiles is outpacing the industrial base that makes them. Washington is responding with record multi-year munitions contracts — Raytheon's $24.4B SM-6 deal being the latest — but those timelines stretch years, leaving Ukraine and Gulf partners short in the interim. Meanwhile the defense map is broadening beyond Washington's control: Saudi Arabia is preparing a Bab el-Mandeb offensive that will test its new Mecca pact with Turkey and Pakistan, and India is quietly locking in Akash buyers in the Caucasus and Central Asia.
sources: Reuters, Korean Central News Agency (via Chosun Biz), Janes, Defence Express (Defence-UA), Army Recognition, AeroTime, TRT World, Associated Press, Al-Monitor, Saudi Gazette, Dawn, The News Mill, Financial Express, Military Watch Magazine, Stars and Stripes, Anadolu Agency, Around Prague (CSG)
